paragraphs: One-sentence judgment: An avionics technician is not a 'parts swapper' but a technical position that installs, inspects, tests, adjusts, and repairs avionics equipment such as radar, radio, navigation, and missile control on aircraft and spacecraft: planning installation from blueprints and manuals and wiring diagrams, installing electrical and electronic components and assemblies and systems, testing and troubleshooting instruments and components and assemblies with circuit testers and oscilloscopes and voltmeters, connecting assemblies such as radio systems and instruments and magnetos and inverters and aerial refueling systems, operating ground support and test equipment to perform functional flight tests, and keeping maintenance and repair records; people who only want to swap parts by feel and are unwilling to be responsible for test data and release conclusions are not suited.

Signals to keep exploring: you can read wiring diagrams and maintenance manuals and use hand tools and soldering irons per procedure, are willing to measure with instruments and record data and the basis for judgments truthfully, can stop and verify when the system status or isolation measures are unclear or when power-on, radio frequency radiation, flammable and explosive hazards, or hazardous energy are involved, and are willing to coordinate work with engineers and other maintenance personnel.

Conditions for pausing investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop of planning — installation — testing — troubleshooting — recording under any supervised conditions, or you can only express interest by 'liking aircraft electronics'; also do not treat being able to solder circuit boards or having done consumer electronics repair as proof that you can independently release aircraft electronic systems. Aircraft maintenance and release, radio frequency and hazardous energy work, and airworthiness release signing must be carried out by personnel with the corresponding authorization according to applicable regulations and institutional procedures with traceable basis retained; this page does not provide installation, testing, repair, or release instructions.

Education and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists 49-2091.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); of the published education composition, 50% require a postsecondary certificate, 18% require a high school diploma or equivalent, and 16% require an associate or other two-year degree; most occupations in this zone require vocational school training, related on-the-job experience, or an associate degree, and require prior related work skills and one to two years of training. On the U.S. side, aircraft maintenance and release are governed by FAA regulations: an organization performing maintenance for others must hold a repair station certificate (14 CFR Part 145), and personnel who supervise and inspect and approve for return to service generally must hold a mechanic or repairman certificate under 14 CFR Part 65. Education, training, industry certification, institutional job qualification, and release authorization are different statuses and must be verified item by item by employer, position, and jurisdiction.

One sentence: This is an avionics technical position that installs per drawings and manuals, troubleshoots by instrument measurement, and is responsible for test data and release conclusions, with the core being planning and installation, testing and troubleshooting, coordination and recording, rather than an interest in electronic products.

The work of avionics technicians can be divided into three categories: installation and assembly (planning the installation of aircraft assemblies and systems from blueprints and manuals and wiring diagrams; using hand tools or soldering irons to connect components to assemblies such as radio systems and instruments and magnetos and inverters and aerial refueling systems; using hand tools and power tools or soldering irons to install electrical and electronic components and assemblies and systems on aircraft; using hand tools or soldering irons to assemble components such as switches and electrical controllers and junction boxes; fabricating parts and test aids as needed; operating computer-aided drafting and design applications to design avionics modification plans; and assembling circuit and instrument and system prototypes or models for testing); testing and troubleshooting (using circuit testers and oscilloscopes or voltmeters to test and troubleshoot instruments and components and assemblies; setting up and operating ground support and test equipment to perform functional flight tests on electrical and electronic systems; interpreting flight test data to diagnose faults and systemic performance problems; and using hand tools or soldering irons to adjust or repair or replace faulty components or assemblies); and coordination and recording (coordinating work with engineers and other technicians and other aircraft maintenance personnel; keeping maintenance and repair work records; and performing the installation and testing and adjustment and repair of avionics equipment in unmanned aerial vehicles such as drones). All three task categories are premised on stopping to verify when the system status or isolation measures are unclear or when power-on, radio frequency, or hazardous energy are involved.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET 49-2091.00 Avionics Technicians (2026 updated page). The official duty is to install, inspect, test, adjust, or repair avionics equipment such as radar, radio, navigation, and missile control systems on aircraft or spacecraft; there are 14 official tasks, 13 Core and 1 New (drone, with no Importance provided), and the summary page does not publish importance scores for the tasks and work activities (the detailed data page gives importance scores for core tasks from 84 to 56). Work activities are listed as 41 items on the detailed data page with importance scores, the highest being documenting and recording information 85, updating and using relevant knowledge 85, getting information 84, repairing and maintaining electronic equipment 83, making decisions and solving problems 79, using computers 79, and evaluating information to determine compliance with standards 78. Detailed work activities are 13 items (no scores). The task list describes the work of the group and does not mean every position performs all the tasks.

entries: Planning and installation | Make the work supported | Plan the installation order of assemblies and systems per blueprints and manuals and wiring diagrams, and write out clearly the basis documents and the wiring and routing.

Connection and assembly | Make the assembly reliable | Use hand tools and power tools or soldering irons to connect and install electrical and electronic components and assemblies and systems, and assemble switches and controllers and junction boxes.

Testing and troubleshooting | Make the judgment supported | Measure with circuit testers and oscilloscopes and voltmeters, set up and operate ground support and test equipment to perform functional tests, and interpret test and flight test data.
Adjustment and replacement | Make the result reviewable | Adjust or repair or replace faulty components or assemblies per procedure, retest, and explain deviations and open items.
Recording and filing | Make the process traceable | Keep maintenance and repair records, recording the basis documents and the measurements and test values and the adjustments and replaced parts.

Collaboration and authorization | Make responsibility attributable | Coordinate with engineers and other maintenance and inspection personnel; when aircraft maintenance and release and radio frequency and hazardous energy are involved, carry them out through the authorized process and report open items truthfully.

paragraphs: Work environment | 69% are in continual contact with others, 66% continually or almost continually use hands to handle and control or feel objects and tools, 64% are exposed to contaminants every day, 62% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day, 58% need face-to-face discussions every day, 40% work indoors in a non-environmentally controlled setting every day, 34% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day, 33% continually or almost continually do repetitive motions, 32% sit more than half the time, 26% never wear common protective or safety equipment. Main equipment and tools | hand tools and soldering irons, circuit testers and oscilloscopes and voltmeters, ground support and test equipment, computer-aided drafting and design software, measurement and calibration instruments, personal protection (goggles, gloves, hearing protection, safety shoes, respiratory protection). Task pace | 79% of typical workweeks are 40 hours; 66% continually use hands to handle and control tools, 33% continually or almost continually do repetitive motions, 32% sit more than half the time; 44% face time pressure at least once a week but not every day. Collaborators | collaborate with design engineers, other avionics technicians, mechanical and structural maintenance personnel, and quality control and inspection personnel; 69% are in continual contact with others, 52% consider working with a work group or team extremely important, 39% have high responsibility for the health and safety of others, 49% consider decisions to be important results for colleagues or the company. Competition and pressure | 37% consider the consequences of error very serious, 61% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 45% have a lot of decision freedom, 32% have some freedom over tasks and priorities and goals, 26% must make decisions every day. Compliance and safety | installation and testing and maintenance must conform to applicable airworthiness and maintenance regulations and institutional procedures; in the U.S., §145.5 requires an operator acting as a certificated repair station to hold a valid certificate, the appropriate ratings, and operations specifications, which cannot be generalized into a requirement that all organizations repairing for others must hold that certificate. §43.3 also allows relevant mechanics, repairmen, qualifying supervised persons, air carriers, or manufacturers, among others, to perform maintenance according to law; the supervised route does not include the inspections specified in Part91/125 and the inspection after major repair or modification. §43.7 return-to-service approval is specified separately by subject and authority, and an ordinary repairman certificate does not automatically confer an independent general release authority. At a certificated repair station within the U.S., §145.153 supervisory personnel and §145.157 personnel authorized to approve for return to service need the applicable Part65 mechanic or repairman certificate; §145.155 ordinary inspection personnel require regulatory, method, tool, and inspection capability, and that provision alone does not imply that all inspectors must hold a Part65 certificate. §145.213 employees who sign the final inspection and maintenance release need the relevant certificate, with an exception for employees of foreign stations. Overseas supervisory or return-to-service personnel have separate training and 18 months of experience and competency conditions, and domestic requirements are not applied uniformly. Records and review | the basis documents and the wiring and the measurements and tests and adjustments and replaced parts need to be traceable; 61% consider precision or accuracy extremely important. Skills and training | O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); basic skills are mainly critical thinking, active listening, speaking, reading comprehension and writing, and monitoring; transferable skills include equipment maintenance, repair, troubleshooting, operations monitoring, and quality control analysis; knowledge is mainly computers and electronics, mechanical, English language, engineering and technology, design, and communications; abilities include written comprehension, information ordering, near vision, oral comprehension, problem sensitivity, deductive reasoning, and finger dexterity (detailed data provide Importance, not frequency). Entry and authorization | education does not equal work or release authorization, and industry certification does not mean one can release aircraft electronic systems at any location; it must follow institutional authorization and applicable regulations. Industry and employers | the O*NET industry distribution for 2025 is manufacturing 38%, transportation and warehousing 37%, other 25%; common employers are aircraft manufacturing and modification organizations, maintenance and repair stations, airline maintenance operations, and drone and spacecraft related organizations. Survey boundary | 26% never wearing common protection is only a group response and cannot be used to cancel actual protection requirements. The new-hire education requirement survey shows 50% postsecondary certificate, 18% high school or equivalent, and 16% associate or other two-year, which is not the on-the-job education composition. Zone3/SVP6 to <7 is a general description, usually one to two years of training, not a fixed number of years for every position; the BLS EP for this occupation, typically postsecondary nondegree award, related experience None, on-the-job training None, is a statistical classification and does not exempt job training or legal qualifications. The OOH combined occupation note says common shifts of 8 or 10 hours including nights, weekends, and holidays, not a fixed schedule for all avionics positions.

Collaborate with design engineers, other avionics technicians, mechanical and structural maintenance personnel, and quality control and inspection personnel; when aircraft power-on and radio frequency radiation and hazardous energy, or airworthiness release signing, are involved, handle them according to applicable regulations and institutional procedures, do not decide on one's own, and stop and escalate when the basis is unclear or the work exceeds authorization.

Avionics technicians focus on the installation and testing and troubleshooting of avionics equipment (radar, radio, navigation, missile control, and so on) on aircraft and spacecraft; aircraft mechanic technicians focus on the maintenance and repair of aircraft mechanical and structural systems and usually cover a wider airframe scope; aerospace engineering and operations technicians focus on engineering support for testing and operations and usually do not undertake release signing; calibration technicians focus on metrology and calibration; commercial and industrial equipment electrical and electronic repairers focus on non-aviation industrial and commercial equipment; transportation equipment electrical and electronic installers focus on non-aviation transport equipment; aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assemblers focus on structure and assembly. Adjacent occupations share tool use and measurement and safety fundamentals, but the object, deliverable, and authorization differ.
A measurable, reviewable, releasable test conclusion

Complete installation and testing and troubleshooting per procedure, and leave a record stating the basis documents and the wiring and measured values, the test data and the basis for the judgment, the adjustments and replaced parts, and the parts that remain uncertain, so that an inspector or reviewer can judge from it.
Installation and testing and maintenance records (including the release basis)

The object is the electrical and electronic systems and equipment on aircraft and spacecraft (radar and radio and navigation and missile control and instruments and communications and aerial refueling systems, and so on); the basis is blueprints and manuals and wiring diagrams, manufacturer technical data, and the applicable airworthiness and maintenance regulations and institutional inspection procedures.

Avionics technicians (O*NET 49-2091.00 on the U.S. side, Avionics Technicians) install, inspect, test, adjust, or repair avionics equipment on aircraft or spacecraft, such as radar, radio, navigation, and missile control systems. The original official duty text is 'Install, inspect, test, adjust, or repair avionics equipment, such as radar, radio, navigation, and missile control systems in aircraft or space vehicles.'; O*NET lists 14 official tasks (all core), including using hand tools or soldering irons to adjust, repair, or replace faulty components or assemblies (importance 84), planning the installation of aircraft assemblies and systems from blueprints and manuals and wiring diagrams (82), keeping maintenance and repair work records (82), using circuit testers and oscilloscopes or voltmeters to test and troubleshoot instruments and components and assemblies (82), using hand tools and soldering irons to connect components to assemblies such as radio systems and instruments and magnetos and inverters and aerial refueling systems (80), installing electrical and electronic components and assemblies and systems on aircraft (78), coordinating work with engineers and technicians and other aircraft maintenance personnel (76), setting up and operating ground support and test equipment to perform functional flight tests on electrical and electronic systems (71), using hand tools or soldering irons to assemble components such as switches and electrical controllers and junction boxes (70), interpreting flight test data to diagnose faults and systemic performance problems (68), fabricating parts and test aids as needed (65), operating computer-aided drafting and design applications to design avionics modification plans (58), and assembling circuit and instrument and system prototypes or models for testing (56), plus one new task — performing the installation, testing, adjustment, and repair of avionics equipment in unmanned aerial vehicles such as drones (no importance score is published for this new task). This occupation is in Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0) in the U.S. This page does not constitute installation, testing, repair, or release instructions; the relevant decisions must be made by personnel with the corresponding qualifications and authorization according to applicable regulations and institutional procedures.
Planning — installation — testing — troubleshooting — recording

Read the basis documents → plan the installation and modification plan → install and wire per procedure → measure and perform functional tests with instruments → interpret the data to locate the fault and adjust or replace → retest and file and explain open items.
A reviewable installation and testing and maintenance record
The basis documents and the wiring and routing, the measured values and test data, the fault and the basis for the judgment, the adjustments and replaced parts, and the parts that remain uncertain.
Self and the inspector (or reviewer)

Installation and testing and troubleshooting conclusions are undertaken by the person according to authorization; when aircraft maintenance and release signing, power-on and radio frequency and hazardous energy work, and airworthiness conformity judgment are involved, they are made by personnel with the corresponding qualifications and authorization according to applicable regulations and procedures, and work must stop and escalate when the basis is unclear or the work exceeds the authorized scope.
Education and preparation

O*NET lists 49-2091.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); most occupations in this zone require vocational school training, related on-the-job experience, or an associate degree, and require prior related work skills, knowledge, or experience, with training usually one to two years and an accredited apprenticeship program possibly available; of the published education composition, 50% require a postsecondary certificate, 18% require a high school diploma or equivalent, and 16% require an associate or other two-year degree. O*NET also lists 3 registered apprenticeship positions (Aircraft Mechanic, Electrical; Avionics Technician; Electrician, Aircraft) and several Avionics Maintenance Technology/Technician training programs; the certification page lists 6 industry certifications (such as the Aircraft Electronics Association's Certified Aircraft Electronics Technician, ASTM International's Aircraft Electronics Technician and Unmanned Aircraft Systems Certification, SpaceTEC's Certified Aerospace Technician, and ETA International's RADAR Electronics Technician, among others). On the mainland China side it is mainly education in avionics and aviation maintenance-related specialties and job training, with specific requirements set by the employer.
Not mutually substitutable

Education, coursework and training, industry certification, registered apprenticeship experience, institutional internal job qualification, and work authorization are different statuses: education does not bring release authorization, and certification does not mean one can independently release aircraft electronic systems or carry out maintenance work at any location; on the U.S. side, an organization performing maintenance for others must hold a repair station certificate, and personnel who supervise and inspect and approve for return to service generally must hold a mechanic or repairman certificate.

At minimum, check six items before onboarding: the occupational definition and the employer entity (O*NET 49-2091.00 is the U.S. definition; on the mainland China side this page obtained no precisely equivalent occupational entry); education and specialized training; institutional internal job qualification and the scope of work authorization; the working procedures for installation and testing and troubleshooting; the qualification requirements for aircraft maintenance and release and radio frequency and hazardous energy work; and the employment arrangement and compensation definition.
Occupational definition

On the U.S. side it is O*NET 49-2091.00 (Avionics Technicians); its wage and employment and industry data are under this occupational definition, and the page does not state that they are taken from another occupation. On the mainland China side this page obtained no public occupational entry precisely equivalent to this occupation, and the Chinese page language does not constitute an equivalent Chinese occupation or a wage mapping; when comparing, first identify whether the position belongs to aircraft manufacturing and modification, a maintenance organization, airline maintenance, or a drone and spacecraft related organization.
Education and specialized pathway

On the U.S. side the education composition is mainly a postsecondary certificate (of the education composition published on the O*NET page, 50% require a postsecondary certificate, 18% require a high school diploma or equivalent, and another 16% require an associate or other two-year degree), and most positions require prior related work skills and one to two years of training, with 3 registered apprenticeship positions and several Avionics Maintenance Technology/Technician training programs; in mainland China it is mainly education in avionics and aviation maintenance-related specialties and job training, with specific education requirements set by the employer.
Job qualification and work authorization

Installation and testing and troubleshooting must follow institutional processes and applicable regulations. On the U.S. side, an organization performing maintenance for others must hold a repair station certificate (14 CFR Part 145, §145.5); supervisory personnel, personnel authorized to approve for return to service, and employees who sign the final inspection and maintenance release must, within the U.S., hold a mechanic or repairman certificate under 14 CFR Part 65 (§145.153, §145.157, §145.213). The O*NET certification page separately lists 6 industry certifications. On the mainland China side this page obtained no precisely equivalent public occupational entry and admission basis, so before onboarding, check pre-job training and work authorization and the release process, which cannot be inferred directly from education or certification.
Equipment and site safety

The working environment must meet applicable safety requirements (hangar and apron and working-at-height and confined-space protection, aircraft power-on and radio frequency radiation and hazardous energy control, welding and soldering iron and chemical and solvent exposure protection, and foreign object and tool and parts management). O*NET work context shows 69% are in continual contact with others, 66% continually or almost continually use hands to handle and control objects and tools, 64% are exposed to contaminants every day, 62% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day, 58% need face-to-face discussions every day, 40% work indoors in a non-environmentally controlled setting every day, 37% consider the consequences of error very serious, 34% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day; this page does not constitute installation, testing, repair, or release instructions.
Shifts and working hours

Work context shows 79% of typical workweeks are 40 hours, 44% face time pressure at least once a week, 45% have a lot of decision freedom, 26% must make decisions every day, 49% consider decisions to be important results for colleagues or the company; common arrangements include hangar and production line and duty shift scheduling and field work. When comparing positions, put the employment arrangement, shifts, and overtime arrangements into the written conditions.
Continuing training and review

Aircraft models and avionics equipment and test equipment and software, as well as airworthiness and maintenance regulations, update fairly quickly (O*NET lists 14 technology skill categories, 12 of them flagged as hot technologies, and the page gives occurrence shares from employer job postings: Microsoft Office 9%, Microsoft Excel 7%, Microsoft Outlook 4%, Microsoft PowerPoint 3%, Microsoft Word 2%, Autodesk AutoCAD 1%, Linux 1%, SAP software 1%, with the rest unpublished), requiring continuous continuing training and maintenance of basis documents; confirm before onboarding the training arrangements, work authorization, and inspection and rework review mechanism.

paragraphs: All six directions share tool use and measurement and safety fundamentals as a background, but the work object and basis and authorization boundary differ; the same segment of electronics or maintenance experience cannot be directly converted into another direction's job qualification, certification, or release authorization, and this page only compares the duty differences under the public definitions.

The comparison basis is the official occupational description of O*NET 49-2091.00 and the related occupation list on the O*NET page, as well as the adjacent occupation relationships noted in the routing material; an adjacent relationship only indicates proximity of duties and does not mean qualifications, certifications, or authorizations are interchangeable.

The table below compares avionics technicians and five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and output, key differences, and which option is more suitable for each preference.

Aircraft mechanic technicians cover a wider range of airframe and powerplant and structural systems and usually involve whole-aircraft maintenance; avionics technicians focus on the installation and testing and troubleshooting of avionics equipment.
If you would rather do whole-aircraft and airframe system maintenance, compare aircraft mechanic technicians first; if you would rather focus on avionics equipment, avionics technicians are suitable.
Maintain and repair aircraft airframe and powerplant and structural systems, with the output mainly being whole-aircraft maintenance and release records.
Avionics technicians and aircraft mechanic technicians

Focuses on engineering support for testing and operations and data analysis and usually does not undertake release signing; avionics technicians focus on equipment installation and testing and troubleshooting and submitting reviewable records.

If you would rather do testing and engineering support, compare aerospace engineering and operations technicians first; if you would rather do equipment installation and troubleshooting, avionics technicians are suitable.
Support testing and operations and deliver test data and engineering analysis records.
Avionics technicians and aerospace engineering and operations technicians
Focuses on metrology and calibration, and the object is various measuring devices; the avionics technician's object is the avionics systems on aircraft and spacecraft.
If you would rather do metrology and calibration, compare calibration technicians first; if you would rather do avionics systems, avionics technicians are suitable.
Perform calibration and metrology of measuring devices, with the output mainly being calibration records and uncertainty notes.
Avionics technicians and calibration technicians
The object is commercial and industrial equipment, usually not involving airworthiness release; the avionics technician's object is avionics equipment on aircraft and spacecraft.

If you would rather do commercial and industrial equipment repair, compare commercial and industrial equipment electrical and electronic repairers first; if you would rather do avionics equipment, avionics technicians are suitable.
Repair commercial and industrial electrical and electronic equipment, with the output mainly being equipment servicing and test records.
Avionics technicians and commercial and industrial equipment electrical and electronic repairers

The object is transport equipment such as rail and ships and motor vehicles, not involving aviation airworthiness regulations; the avionics technician's object is avionics equipment on aircraft and spacecraft.

If you would rather do electrical and electronic work on non-aviation transport equipment, compare transportation equipment electrical and electronic installers first; if you would rather do avionics equipment, avionics technicians are suitable.
Install and maintain the electrical and electronic systems of transport equipment, with the output mainly being installation and servicing records.
Avionics technicians and transportation equipment electrical and electronic installers

Focuses on the assembly and rigging of structures and surfaces and usually does not involve avionics system testing; avionics technicians focus on the installation and testing of electrical and electronic systems.
If you would rather do structure and assembly, compare aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assemblers first; if you would rather do avionics systems, avionics technicians are suitable.
Assemble aircraft structures and surfaces and rigging and systems, with the output mainly being assembly and inspection records.
Avionics technicians and aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assemblers

Conclusion: The basis for choosing a direction is the work object and basis and authorization boundary, not whether electronics are involved; once the direction is set, the target direction's training, certification, job qualification, or release authorization requirements should be checked item by item.

entries.answer: Install, inspect, test, adjust, or repair avionics equipment on aircraft and spacecraft: plan the installation from blueprints and manuals and wiring diagrams, install electrical and electronic components and assemblies and systems, test and troubleshoot with circuit testers and oscilloscopes and voltmeters, connect assemblies such as radio systems and instruments and magnetos and inverters, set up and operate ground support and test equipment to perform functional tests, interpret flight test data to locate faults, and keep maintenance and repair records.
entries.question: What do avionics technicians do every day?

entries.answer: Mainly aircraft power-on and radio frequency radiation and hazardous energy, welding and soldering iron and chemical and solvent exposure, system failure from mis-wiring and improper installation, leakage of aircraft model and maintenance and test data, misjudging test conditions and calibration status, and unauthorized release and unclear work authorization; the control approach is to work per applicable regulations and institutional procedures and to stop and escalate when the basis is unclear or the work exceeds authorization.
entries.question: What risks should I pay attention to in advance with this job?

entries.answer: Look at reviewable output: whether you can complete installation and testing and troubleshooting per procedure and record truthfully, whether you can reason about faults and conformity from the basis documents and measurement data, and whether you can stop and escalate when the basis is unclear or the work exceeds authorization. The RCI interest code and work styles only indicate that the direction is close and cannot replace this hands-on evidence.
entries.question: How do I judge whether I am suited to being an avionics technician?

entries.answer: AI and automation can change basis document retrieval and manual lookup, measurement records and parameter comparison, and the organization of installation and testing and maintenance records; but wiring and installation quality judgment, fault cause location, and test and release conclusions are still undertaken by the person per institutional procedures and applicable regulations. Main sources: O*NET49-2091 details, wages, industry, Hot, trend, and training and certification directories; BLS EP and the separate OOH avionics statistics; eCFR §43.3/7/13, §145.5/109/153/155/157/213 and §65.101/103; China's 2022 Occupational Classification Code, the 2025 revision of the Civil Aviation Law, and the NBS2025 industry wages.

Data dates: O*NET2026 update, wages 2025 OEWS, hiring software 2025, employment 2025 and 2025—2035. The specific eCFR provisions were read this round, with titles current to 2026-10-07 and not the revision date of each provision; China's Civil Aviation Law takes effect 2026-07-01, classification 2022, industry wages 2025. The original MOHRSS old text was not successfully obtained this round, and search snippets are not treated as verified full text.

Boundary: U.S. statistics are for this occupation 49-2091, and the OOH combined occupation and the aircraft mechanic row must be kept separate; the Chinese related duties are not precise mutual recognition, and the industry averages do not fill the occupational monthly wage gap; maintenance, ordinary inspection, supervision and final signing, and domestic and overseas stations each have their authority checked separately. Directories and editorial suggestions are not a complete working procedure or a universal hiring standard.

hero.quick_answer: Avionics technicians install, inspect, test, adjust, or repair avionics equipment on aircraft and spacecraft (radar and radio and navigation and missile control, and so on): planning the installation from blueprints and manuals and wiring diagrams, installing electrical and electronic components and assemblies and systems, testing and troubleshooting with circuit testers and oscilloscopes and voltmeters, setting up and operating ground support and test equipment to perform functional tests, and interpreting flight test data and keeping records; their work does not equal airframe and powerplant system repair, nor does it replace aircraft maintenance release signing and the authorization determination related to power-on and radio frequency and hazardous energy, and they stop and escalate when the system status is unclear or the work exceeds authorization.

subject.name: Avionics Technicians
subject.summary: Avionics technicians install, inspect, test, adjust, or repair avionics equipment on aircraft and spacecraft (radar, radio, navigation, missile control, and so on): planning and installing per basis documents, measuring and testing and troubleshooting with instruments, setting up ground support equipment to perform functional tests, and keeping maintenance records. On the U.S. side this corresponds to O*NET 49-2091.00 (Avionics Technicians), in Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); the wage and employment and industry data are all under this occupational definition. On the mainland China side this page obtained no public occupational entry and national wage distribution precisely corresponding to this occupation, using only the MOHRSS intermediate occupational class as a proxy, and the Chinese page language does not constitute an equivalent Chinese occupation or a wage mapping.
